MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN)   -- Mexicans in the United States sent home 12.2 percent less money this past August than the same month last year, the Banco de Mexico said Wednesday. Mexicans in the U.S. are sending fewer dollars home and are suffering from a tough economy. That translates into remittances of $1.9 billion, versus $2.2 billion last year, said the bank, which blamed tough economic times in the United States for the decline. "The prolonged deceleration of economic activity in the United States has adversely affected the opportunities for employment in that country and, consequently, those of the Mexican migrants," the bank said in a statement posted on its Web site. August's tally quickens a trend -- during the first eight months of the year, remittances fell 4 percent to $15.6 billion, the statement said. The numbers translate easily into stories of hardship. Marilyn Pena lives outside Mexico City and depends on remittances to get by. Her father migrated to Chicago 12 years ago to find work and, in good months, sends his daughter about $200 per week. But last week he sent nothing. "He told me he has no more work because of the situation there," Pena said. "Temporary workers are always the first to lose their jobs in crises like this one," said Luis Pena, an economist. "Since many Mexicans in the United States are there illegally, they are most vulnerable to unemployment." Some economists predict the drop will increase by year's end to 20 percent. After oil exports, remittances are Mexico's second-largest source of foreign currency. In Atlanta, Georgia, which has one of the greatest concentrations of Mexican residents in the southeastern United States, Yasmin Gutierrez runs a company that Mexican immigrants use to send dollars abroad. "Before, they used to come every week and they used to send big amounts and lately, well, nothing, or almost nothing. Some clients are no longer coming, and those that are coming are sending small amounts." Rosina Gonzalez, who ran a Western Union office in Atlanta several years ago and recently returned to the job, said she has noticed a big change. Back then, "everyone was sending money to Mexico, Mexico, Mexico -- a lot of money," she said. "Now, I'm returning to work after four or five years and the norm now is that the people who used to send money to Mexico are asking the people in Mexico to send money here." Some are abandoning their hope for a slice of the American dream by opting to return to their country. The woman running the foreign-currency exchange service Afex, also in Atlanta, said business is so bad she is afraid of losing her job. CNN's Harris Whitbeck in Mexico City and Viviana Fernandez in Atlanta contributed to this story.

MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN) -- Money transfers from Mexicans living in the United States to relatives back home fell by 12.2 percent in August compared with the same month a year earlier, Banco de Mexico reported Wednesday.

Mexican migrants in the U.S. are sending less money as they struggle with a weak economy. The decline brought August remittances to $1.9 billion, down from $2.2 billion the previous year, according to the bank, which attributed the drop to difficult economic conditions in the United States.

“The prolonged deceleration of economic activity in the United States has adversely affected the opportunities for employment in that country and, consequently, those of the Mexican migrants,” the bank said in a statement published on its Web site.

The August figure shows the downturn is accelerating. Over the first eight months of the year, remittances decreased 4 percent, totaling $15.6 billion, the statement said.

Behind the figures are personal stories of financial strain. Marilyn Pena, who lives near Mexico City, relies on money sent from abroad to cover her expenses. Her father moved to Chicago 12 years ago in search of employment and, when times are good, sends her about $200 a week. Last week, however, he sent nothing.

“He told me he has no more work because of the situation there,” Pena said.

Luis Pena, an economist, said temporary laborers are usually the first to be dismissed during economic crises. “Since many Mexicans in the United States are there illegally, they are most vulnerable to unemployment,” he said.

Some economists expect the decline in remittances to reach 20 percent by the end of the year.

Remittances are Mexico’s second-biggest source of foreign currency, after oil exports.

In Atlanta, Georgia, home to one of the largest Mexican populations in the southeastern United States, Yasmin Gutierrez operates a business that Mexican immigrants use to send money overseas.

“Before, they used to come every week and they used to send big amounts and lately, well, nothing, or almost nothing,” she said. “Some clients are no longer coming, and those that are coming are sending small amounts.”

Rosina Gonzalez, who managed a Western Union branch in Atlanta several years ago and has recently gone back to the job, said the difference is striking. In the past, she said, “everyone was sending money to Mexico, Mexico, Mexico -- a lot of money.” Now, after returning to work following four or five years away, she said the situation has reversed: people who once sent money to Mexico are now asking relatives there to send money to the United States.

Others are giving up on their pursuit of the American dream and choosing to go back to Mexico.

The woman who operates Afex, a foreign-currency exchange service in Atlanta, said business has fallen so sharply that she fears she could lose her job.

CNN’s Harris Whitbeck in Mexico City and Viviana Fernandez in Atlanta contributed to this report.

*Note: The article below is written in a TV-news-style format, but it does not imitate CNN’s exact voice. Quotes from families and businesses are presented as clearly labeled composite examples, not real interviews.*

---

## Remittances to Mexico fall as economic downturn hits Mexican workers in U.S.

**MEXICO CITY** — For years, money sent home by Mexicans living in the United States helped pay for groceries, school fees, medicine and home repairs across Mexico. But as the U.S. economy slowed and job losses mounted, that financial lifeline weakened.

According to **Banco de México**, remittances to Mexico fell sharply during the downturn. After reaching about **$26 billion in 2007**, remittances declined to roughly **$25.1 billion in 2008** and dropped further in **2009 to about $21.2 billion**, a decrease of more than **15% from the previous year**. It marked one of the steepest declines since Mexico began tracking remittances closely.

Economists say the drop reflected the struggles of Mexican migrants working in sectors hit hard by the recession, including construction, manufacturing, hospitality and agriculture.

For families in rural communities, the impact was immediate.

“We used to count on money every month from my brother in California,” said **María López**, a composite example of families affected in Michoacán, one of the states that relies heavily on remittances. “Now he sends what he can, but sometimes nothing comes. We have had to cut back on food, medicine and repairs to the house.”

Remittances are one of Mexico’s largest sources of foreign income, often rivaling revenue from oil exports and foreign direct investment. The money is especially important in states such as Michoacán, Guanajuato, Jalisco, Zacatecas and Oaxaca, where migration to the United States has long shaped local economies.

Money-transfer businesses also felt the downturn.

“At the worst point, we saw fewer customers and smaller transfers,” said **Javier Hernández**, a composite money-transfer operator in Los Angeles. “People who used to send $300 or $400 were sending $100, or they were waiting two or three months before sending anything.”

Banco de México data showed not only a decline in the total amount sent, but also pressure on the average size of transfers. Analysts said many migrants were still sending money, but in smaller amounts and less frequently.

The fall in remittances was tied closely to job losses in the United States. Mexican migrants, particularly those without legal status, were vulnerable because many worked in industries that contracted quickly during the economic crisis. Construction jobs disappeared as the housing market collapsed, and service-sector work became more difficult to find.

In Mexico, the decline rippled through local communities.

“Before, the money from the United States helped us pay for my daughter’s school expenses,” said **Rosa Martínez**, a composite mother in Guanajuato. “When the transfers stopped, we had to borrow from relatives and delay payments.”

Small businesses in towns dependent on migrant income also reported weaker sales.

“When families receive remittances, they buy food, clothing, building materials,” said **Carlos Ramírez**, a composite shop owner in Zacatecas. “When the money stops coming, the whole town feels it.”

Despite the decline, analysts noted that remittances did not disappear. Many migrants continued to send money even while facing unemployment or reduced hours, underscoring the strength of family obligations across the border.

“Remittances are not just an economic transaction,” said one Mexico-based migration analyst. “They are part of a survival strategy for millions of households.”

The downturn also highlighted Mexico’s dependence on income earned abroad. While remittances help reduce poverty and support local consumption, economists warn that communities relying heavily on money from migrants are vulnerable when the U.S. economy slows.

For families like López’s, the numbers from Banco de México reflect a personal reality.

“When the money arrives, we breathe a little easier,” she said. “When it doesn’t, we just hope next month will be better.”

Remittances are one of Mexico’s most important sources of foreign income, alongside oil revenue, tourism and manufacturing exports. For millions of households, they are also a vital safety net. But as the U.S. economy has weakened, many migrants have found it harder to send the same amount of money home — or to send money at all.

Economists say the drop reflects both the depth of the U.S. recession and the concentration of Mexican migrant labor in sectors hit especially hard by the downturn. Construction, once a major employer of Mexican workers in the United States, has suffered steep job losses following the collapse of the housing market. Other migrants working in hotels, landscaping, food service and domestic labor have also seen income fall.

The August decline is part of a broader downward trend in money transfers to Mexico. Families that once received regular monthly payments are increasingly reporting smaller deposits, longer gaps between transfers or no payments in some months. In communities heavily dependent on migration, local businesses are feeling the effect as households cut back on purchases and postpone repairs, celebrations and investment in small enterprises.

For Mexico, the fall in remittances adds pressure to an economy already weakened by lower exports, reduced investment and declining oil income. Analysts warn that reduced cash flows from migrants could deepen poverty in some regions, particularly in states with long migration histories such as Michoacán, Guanajuato, Jalisco, Zacatecas and Oaxaca.

The decline also highlights the close economic ties between Mexico and the United States. While remittances are private transfers between workers and families, they have become a major part of Mexico’s economic landscape. When employment conditions deteriorate north of the border, the effects are quickly felt in Mexican towns thousands of miles away.

Despite the drop, migrants continue to send billions of dollars home each month, showing the strength of family obligations even in difficult times. But with the U.S. labor market still weak, specialists say remittances are unlikely to recover quickly.

**Mexican remittances fall as U.S. job losses squeeze migrant workers**

**MEXICO CITY/ATLANTA —** For years, the money arrived on the same Friday afternoon.

From Atlanta, where her son worked long shifts in construction, María Elena Rodríguez would receive a transfer of $250 or $300 every two weeks — enough to help cover rent, medicine and groceries in the eastern edge of Mexico City.

But last month, the deposit was half its usual size. This month, it did not come at all.

“He told me, ‘Mamá, I’m sorry. There’s no work right now,’” Rodríguez said, standing outside a neighborhood money-transfer office where fewer customers than usual waited in line. “I know he wants to help. But if he doesn’t earn, he can’t send.”

Across Mexico, families who depend on money sent home by relatives in the United States are feeling the strain as job losses and reduced hours among migrant workers begin to cut into remittances — one of the country’s most important sources of foreign income and a lifeline for millions of households.

Economists say the slowdown is tied to weakening employment in U.S. sectors that rely heavily on immigrant labor, including construction, restaurants, cleaning services, landscaping and hospitality. Many Mexican migrants work in jobs with little security, few benefits and limited savings, making them among the first to be affected when demand drops.

In Atlanta, José Luis Hernández, a 38-year-old from Puebla, said he had spent nearly a decade sending money to his parents every month. The funds helped pay for his father’s diabetes treatment and repairs to the family home.

Now, after the roofing company where he worked cut crews, Hernández has been picking up occasional day labor jobs outside hardware stores.

“Before, I could send $400 without thinking too much,” he said. “Now I have to choose between sending money and paying my own rent.”

He said several friends have stopped sending remittances altogether.

“It’s not that people forgot their families,” Hernández said. “It’s that people here are also afraid.”

Remittances have become a cornerstone of Mexico’s economy, often surpassing oil revenues and foreign direct investment. The money reaches both rural towns and major cities, supporting household consumption, education, health care and small businesses. In some communities, nearly every family has at least one relative working in the United States.

A decline can ripple quickly.

In Mexico City’s Iztapalapa borough, shop owner Claudia Mendoza said some customers who used to pay cash after receiving money from relatives abroad are now asking for credit.

“They tell me, ‘My son didn’t send this week,’ or ‘My husband only sent a little,’” Mendoza said from behind the counter of her small grocery store. “So they buy less — fewer eggs, less meat, cheaper brands.”

Money-transfer businesses are also noticing the change. At one branch near a busy market in the capital, an employee who declined to give his name because he was not authorized to speak publicly said transactions had slowed, particularly transfers from states such as Georgia, Texas and California.

“People still come, but some say the amount is smaller,” he said. “A few are asking if there’s a fee discount.”

Analysts caution that remittance flows can fluctuate month to month and are influenced by exchange rates, inflation and seasonal labor patterns. But they say a sustained fall would put pressure on Mexican households already dealing with higher living costs.

“For many families, remittances are not extra income — they are basic income,” said a Mexico City-based economist who studies migration and household spending. “When that money declines, the immediate response is to cut consumption, delay medical care or take on debt.”

The impact is also emotional.

Rodríguez said she worries less about the missing money than about her son’s life in the United States. He shares an apartment with other workers outside Atlanta and has told her he is avoiding expenses, eating cheaper meals and looking for jobs wherever he can.

“He says he’s fine, but a mother knows,” she said. “If he isn’t sending, it’s because things are very bad.”

In Atlanta, migrant advocacy groups say more workers are seeking help with rent, food and legal questions after losing jobs or seeing hours reduced. Some undocumented migrants are reluctant to apply for assistance or report wage theft, fearing contact with authorities.

“People are trying to survive quietly,” said one community organizer who works with Latino families in the Atlanta area. “They have obligations here and obligations back home. When work disappears, the pressure comes from both sides of the border.”

For Hernández, the hardest call each month is to his mother in Puebla.

“She always says, ‘Don’t worry about us,’” he said. “But I know they do worry. And I worry too.”

Back in Mexico City, Rodríguez folded a receipt from her last remittance transfer and slipped it into her purse. She said she has started stretching meals, buying fewer medicines at once and postponing a utility payment.

She still waits for her son’s message every Friday.

“Before, I waited for the money,” she said. “Now I wait just to hear he found work.”

**Banco de México Reports Decline in Remittances From U.S., Stirring Concern in Migrant-Dependent Communities**

*By Staff Writer*

**MEXICO CITY** — Banco de México has reported a decline in remittances sent by Mexicans living in the United States, a shift that is raising concern in communities across Mexico where money transfers from abroad help pay for food, housing, education, medical care and small businesses.

The central bank’s latest figures show that remittance inflows have weakened after years of strong growth, reflecting a combination of economic pressures facing Mexican migrants in the United States and changing conditions in Mexico. Economists say the slowdown does not necessarily point to a collapse in migrant earnings, but it does suggest that households on both sides of the border are adjusting to higher costs, tighter job markets in some sectors and uncertainty about the U.S. economy.

For families who depend on those transfers, even a modest decline can be felt immediately.

“Before, my brother sent money every two weeks without fail,” said **María Elena Torres**, a resident of a small town in Michoacán whose brother works in construction in California. “Now he sends less, and sometimes he waits three or four weeks. He tells us rent is higher, gasoline is higher, and there isn’t always work. We understand, but here that money pays for my mother’s medicines.”

Remittances have become one of Mexico’s most important sources of foreign income, surpassing earnings from several traditional export sectors in recent years. The transfers are especially vital in states with long histories of migration, including Michoacán, Jalisco, Guanajuato, Zacatecas, Oaxaca, Puebla and Guerrero.

### U.S. inflation and job uncertainty weigh on migrants

Analysts say one of the main causes of the decline is the financial strain on Mexican workers in the United States, many of whom are employed in construction, agriculture, hospitality, domestic work, food service and manufacturing.

Although U.S. inflation has moderated from its recent peaks, prices for rent, utilities, insurance, food and transportation remain significantly higher than before the pandemic. For migrants who often support two households — one in the United States and another in Mexico — the pressure has reduced the amount available to send home.

“Remittances are usually very resilient because migrants prioritize their families,” said **Dr. Andrés Villalobos**, an economist specializing in migration and household finance. “But resilience has limits. If a worker’s rent rises by $300 a month, if car insurance increases, if overtime hours disappear, that money has to come from somewhere. Often it comes out of what would have been sent to Mexico.”

Construction, a major employer of Mexican migrants, has shown uneven performance in parts of the United States as high interest rates have affected housing affordability and delayed some projects. In agriculture and hospitality, seasonal employment patterns and regional slowdowns have also contributed to irregular earnings.

“For many workers, it is not that they have stopped sending money,” Villalobos added. “It is that they are sending smaller amounts, or sending less frequently.”

### Strong peso reduces value for recipients

Another factor is the strength of the Mexican peso against the U.S. dollar. When the peso appreciates, each dollar sent from the United States converts into fewer pesos for families in Mexico.

That exchange-rate effect can change household budgets even if the amount sent in dollars remains the same.

“If someone used to send $300 and the exchange rate was more favorable, the family could stretch that money further,” said **Lucía Hernández**, a financial analyst in Mexico City. “When the peso is stronger, the same $300 buys fewer pesos. Families may perceive a decline even when the migrant is making the same sacrifice.”

A stronger peso has benefits for Mexico, including helping reduce the cost of imports and signaling investor confidence. But for families dependent on remittances, it can feel like a pay cut.

“In my house, we calculate everything in pesos,” said **Rosa Isela Martínez**, whose husband works in Texas and sends money to their family in Guanajuato. “He says, ‘I sent the same dollars,’ and I know that is true. But here, the money does not cover the same expenses. School supplies, eggs, tortillas, medicine — everything adds up.”

### Remittance businesses see smaller transactions

Money-transfer companies and small remittance agencies say they have noticed a change in customer behavior. Some migrants are still sending money regularly, but in smaller amounts. Others are waiting longer between transfers.

“At the counter, you can hear the worry,” said **Jorge Ramírez**, manager of a remittance service in Los Angeles that serves customers from Michoacán, Oaxaca and Guerrero. “People used to send $400 or $500. Now some send $250 and say, ‘I’ll send the rest next week if I get more hours.’ They are not forgetting their families. They are stretched.”

In Mexico, local businesses that serve remittance-receiving households are also watching closely. In many towns, remittances circulate quickly through grocery stores, pharmacies, construction suppliers, school payments and local services.

“When remittances slow down, you see it almost immediately,” said **Ana Patricia Gómez**, who operates a payment and transfer agency in Puebla. “People withdraw less. They ask about the exchange rate more. Some tell us they are waiting because their son or daughter in the U.S. did not get paid enough that week.”

### Families delay repairs, education expenses

The decline is affecting decisions inside households. Some families are postponing home improvements, medical appointments or educational expenses. Others are cutting back on nonessential purchases.

In rural communities, remittances often help finance planting costs, livestock feed or small shops. A smaller transfer can mean a delayed investment or more reliance on local credit.

“My father wanted to repair the roof before the rains,” said **José Luis Cabrera**, a teacher in Oaxaca whose siblings live in Illinois. “But my brothers told us they cannot send as much right now. So we are waiting. It is not an emergency yet, but it shows how dependent we are on money from the north.”

Economists note that remittances are frequently used for consumption rather than large-scale investment, but that consumption is essential to household stability.

“It is easy to talk about remittances as a macroeconomic number,” said Hernández. “But at the family level, remittances are food, electricity, doctor visits and transportation. A decline of even 5 or 10 percent can be very important for a low-income household.”

### Migration costs and debt also play a role

Experts say newer migrants may also be sending less because many face debts related to migration costs, including transportation, legal fees or payments to intermediaries. Those obligations can reduce the amount available for family support during the first months or years abroad.

Meanwhile, tighter immigration enforcement in some areas can create additional costs and insecurity. Workers without stable legal status may avoid changing jobs, reporting wage theft or seeking better pay, all of which can affect income.

“There is a hidden cost to uncertainty,” said Villalobos. “If a migrant is worried about losing work, being detained or not being able to travel, they may keep more cash in the United States as a precaution instead of sending everything home.”

### Banks and transfer firms compete for cautious customers

The remittance market has become increasingly competitive, with banks, digital platforms, convenience stores and traditional transfer companies all seeking customers. Lower fees and mobile apps have made it easier to send money, but companies say the current challenge is not access — it is the amount migrants can afford to transfer.

“We have more digital users than before, but the average transaction has softened,” said **Carolina Méndez**, regional director for a remittance platform serving U.S.-Mexico corridors. “Customers are comparing exchange rates and fees more carefully. A few pesos can matter when families are under pressure.”

Some businesses are promoting lower-cost transfers, loyalty discounts and better exchange-rate guarantees. But industry representatives acknowledge that cheaper fees cannot fully offset weaker earnings.

“If a customer has only $200 available, we can help make the transfer efficient,” Méndez said. “But we cannot solve the fact that their paycheck is smaller or their rent is higher.”

### Broader impact on Mexico’s economy

At the national level, remittances remain a major support for Mexico’s economy, especially in lower-income regions. They help sustain consumption, reduce poverty and provide foreign currency inflows. A continued decline could weigh on local economies, particularly in towns where migration is central to household income.

Still, economists caution against overreacting to a single report.

“Monthly remittance figures can be volatile,” said Villalobos. “There are seasonal patterns, exchange-rate effects and one-time factors. The key question is whether this becomes a sustained trend.”

If the decline continues, it could complicate the finances of households already dealing with higher prices in Mexico. Although inflation in Mexico has eased from previous highs, many families say basic goods remain expensive.

“For people receiving remittances, the problem is double,” said Hernández. “They may receive fewer dollars, and those dollars may convert into fewer pesos, while prices remain elevated.”

### Communities remain dependent on migrants’ sacrifices

In many migrant-sending towns, the emotional weight of the decline is as important as the financial one. Families are careful not to blame relatives abroad, knowing that migrants often live frugally to support loved ones in Mexico.

“My son tells me he is eating less outside and sharing an apartment with more people,” said **Carmen Aguilar**, whose son works in a restaurant in Arizona. “He apologizes when he sends less. I tell him not to apologize. He is doing what he can.”

Local leaders say the report should be a reminder that remittances, while vital, are not a substitute for job creation in Mexico.

“We are grateful for what migrants send, but our towns cannot depend forever on people leaving,” said **Miguel Ángel Reyes**, a community organizer in Zacatecas. “When remittances fall, we see how fragile the system is. Families need opportunities here too.”

For now, families are adjusting — stretching budgets, delaying purchases and waiting for conditions to improve in the United States.

“My brother says work may pick up again in a few months,” Torres said. “We hope so. But we also know life there is hard. Every dollar he sends has a story behind it.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN news segment transcript/article on the impact of the U.S. economic slowdown on Mexican workers sending money home, mentioning Atlanta money-transfer offices, vulnerable undocumented workers, and predictions of a 20% drop by year’s end.
counterfactuals.output:
**CNN-style news segment transcript/article**

**ANCHOR:**  
For millions of families in Mexico, money sent home by relatives working in the United States is a lifeline — helping pay for food, rent, school fees and medical care. But as the U.S. economy slows, those remittances are under pressure. Economists and community advocates warn that money transfers could fall sharply by the end of the year, with some predicting a drop of as much as 20%.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
At money-transfer offices in Atlanta, the signs of strain are increasingly visible. Workers who once came in every week to wire earnings back to Mexico are now sending less — or waiting longer between transfers.

Many Mexican workers in the U.S. are employed in industries hit hard by the slowdown, including construction, restaurants, landscaping, hospitality and domestic work. When hours are cut or jobs disappear, the first impact is often felt not only in American households, but in towns and villages across Mexico.

For undocumented workers, the situation is especially vulnerable. Without legal status, many have limited access to unemployment benefits, workplace protections or government assistance. Some are reluctant to report wage theft or unsafe working conditions, fearing that drawing attention could put them at risk of deportation.

**WORKER, ATLANTA:**  
“Before, I sent money every Friday. Now maybe every two weeks, sometimes once a month. My family depends on it, but I don’t have the same hours.”

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Remittances are one of Mexico’s most important sources of foreign income, often surpassing revenue from tourism and rivaling major export sectors. In many rural communities, the money sent from the U.S. helps sustain local economies — supporting small shops, schools and families who rely on relatives abroad.

But transfer agencies say customers are sending smaller amounts. Some workers are choosing between paying rent in the U.S. and supporting relatives back home.

**MONEY-TRANSFER OFFICE EMPLOYEE:**  
“We still see people come in, but the amounts are lower. Someone who used to send $300 may now send $150. Some tell us they lost their job or their hours were cut.”

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Analysts say the slowdown is creating a ripple effect. A construction worker in Georgia loses overtime; a family in Michoacán cuts back on groceries. A restaurant employee in Atlanta misses a shift; school expenses in Oaxaca go unpaid.

Several forecasts now suggest remittances to Mexico could decline significantly by year’s end — with some economists warning of a possible 20% drop if job losses continue in sectors that depend heavily on immigrant labor.

**ECONOMIST:**  
“When the U.S. economy slows, migrant workers are often among the first affected. Because so many remittances come from low-wage employment, even a small reduction in hours can translate into a major loss for families in Mexico.”

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Community organizations say undocumented workers face a double burden: fewer job opportunities and fewer safety nets. Many continue working despite lower wages because their families depend on every dollar they can send.

**ANCHOR:**  
And as the slowdown deepens, the impact will not stop at the border. For families across Mexico, the shrinking flow of money from the United States could mean difficult choices — and a long year ahead.
